wine.name: Vinha Barrosa
wine.appellation: Vinho Regional, outside the Bairrada DOC
wine.grapes: Baga alone, from vines planted, by the house's account, in 1900.
wine.sites: Vinha Barrosa, a single vineyard of old Baga worked by hand on chalky clay, barro meaning clay, and ringed by pine and eucalyptus; the house holds it alone.
wine.making: Destemmed and fermented on its skins for about two weeks, in temperature controlled stainless steel vats in the vintages of the 2010s, then aged in new and used oak: about a year in Allier casks in those vintages, and two years in Portuguese and French oak for the 2021.
wine.glass: Red plum and sour cherry with tobacco and a cool note of mint; dense, firm tannin and bright, unashamed acidity carry a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and firm in youth, it needs several years in bottle, and from a strong vintage it lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard of old Baga the wine comes from; vinha means vineyard.
A vineyard held whole by one house, a word on this label since the late 2000s.
A regional wine rather than DOC Bairrada, the house's choice from the 1999 vintage, named Beiras on the early labels.
The grape: late ripening and small berried, high in acid and in tannin.

records.table: Luís Pato's Vinha Barrosa is Baga alone from a single vineyard on clay, planted by the house's account in 1900. Expect sour cherry, tobacco and mint over firm tannin and bright acidity, and decant it before roast meats.
records.story: The family's roots in Bairrada wine run deep: by the house's own account, records of 1887 already named its ancestors among the region's leading growers. In 1970 the founder's father began to bottle wine from his own vineyards, among the first growers of the Bairrada to do so. In 1980 the son made his first wine, a red of Baga alone, and he went on to argue for Baga as a fine grape rather than a rough one. In 1995 the house launched its single vineyard reds, Vinha Barrosa, Vinha Pan and Quinta do Ribeirinho Pé Franco among them. From the 1999 vintage it labelled its wines as regional wines of the Beiras rather than DOC Bairrada, a protest, as the founder has told it, at the man the government had put at the head of the region's body. Vinha Barrosa, planted in 1900 by the house's account, has carried the word Monopólio on its label since the late 2000s, the vineyard being the house's alone. For a sommelier it is the old vine face of Baga: a red of one place that shows what the grape becomes with time.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's share of 35, three on the house's own domain; one fetch of luispato.com tried and refused, not retried.

The house's vineyards page gives Vinha Barrosa planted in 1900, worked by hand, ringed by pine and eucalyptus, Monopólio on the label after the 2008 vintage, and the single vineyard wines of 1995; merchants give the vines as 70, 80 or more than 100 years old, so the record keeps the house's year and says so.

The clay rests on two importers' estate notes (Grossberg Kopman Selections, VWM), a tasting note republished on the house's site and the name itself (barro, clay); the Allier oak and about a year rest on Cave Lusa and Apewineboxes, with a 2021 listing of two years in Portuguese and French oak, so the making says longer in some vintages.

The label category is the open point: the house chose Vinho Regional Beiras from the 1999 vintage (Uncorked, Skurnik, Wine Enthusiast's 2001 Beiras listing), and Barrosa listings of 2018 and 2021 still say Beiras, but the IVV names Beira Atlântico as the Bairrada's IGP and some recent Pato wines are listed as Beira Atlântico, so the appellation field says Vinho Regional, outside the Bairrada DOC, rather than name one IGP.
Uncorked says the house returned to DOC Bairrada in 2008 while Skurnik says it labels as Regional Beiras since 1999; the return is left out.

Left out for want of a second source: the last plot of Barrosa bought in 2007 (one importer), destemming since 1984 (a writer's blog), the Baga Friends group, the Panasqueira vineyard of 1980 as Vinha Pan, and the winery's move to Amoreira da Gândara (an importer named for a person).

The father's bottling of 1970, the Rota da Bairrada's account, is told as among the first rather than the first; the library calls the Pé Franco the region's benchmark, a judgement word the record does not repeat.
Living names met, none in the prose: the founder, his daughter and the writers whose notes the house republishes.

wine.name: Frei João Reserva Tinto
wine.grapes: Baga alone in the old cellar vintages; recent Reservas are mostly Baga, with Touriga Nacional for the rest.
wine.sites: Baga from the clay of the Bairrada; in the early 1970s the house bought and replanted its own estate, Quinta do Poço do Lobo, near Cantanhede.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented on its skins; after the malolactic fermentation the wine spends about six months in French oak casks and, in the vintages of the 2010s, about eighteen months more in cement vats before bottling. The house keeps back wine of the vintages it judges strongest, releasing old bottles decades on.
wine.glass: Sour cherry and red plum when young, with firm, rustic tannin and high acidity; with decades in bottle it turns to dried cherry, tobacco, forest floor and leather, its acidity keeping it fresh.
wine.ageing: Rustic and firm when young, it was made to wait: the house has released Frei João Reserva from vintages as old as the 1960s.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead, and stand an old one upright and pour it gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house's brand for its Bairrada wines, born at the end of the 1950s.

records.table: Frei João is the Bairrada red of Caves São João, a family house near Anadia founded in 1920. Baga led, it is firm and tart in youth, and the house keeps bottles back for decades, so an old vintage shows how long Baga can live.
records.story: In 1920 three brothers of the Costa family founded the business at São João da Azenha, near Anadia, at first to trade in fine Douro wines and liqueurs, by the house's own account. The firm turned to the wines of its own region, and towards the end of the 1950s it launched the brand that made its name, Frei João. The house claims to have been the first to put the word Reserva on its wines, and it dressed its bottles in paper labels coated with natural cork. In the early 1970s it bought and replanted Quinta do Poço do Lobo near Cantanhede, and the Bairrada itself was recognised and demarcated only by an order of 28 December 1979. Above all the house kept back wine of the vintages it judged strongest for future generations, so its cellars hold reds and whites from the 1960s on, and Frei João Reserva has been released from vintages such as 1966, 1970 and 1985. Those old Baga reds, rustic and tart when young, came out of the cellar earthy and fresh after decades. For a sommelier an old Frei João is the proof of what Baga does with time, and a bottle that teaches patience.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35, two on the house's own domain.

The founding of 1920 by three Costa brothers rests on the house's history page and a merchant (Wine from Portugal), who name them José, Manuel and Albano; their dates were not found, so they are described, not named, and the Sociedade dos Vinhos Irmãos Unidos company name (Blend All About Wine and a competition listing) and the name Caves São João from 1950 (Blend alone) are left out.

Frei João's grapes: the 1985 is Baga alone by Spirited Wines and Olé and Obrigado, the 2014 Reserva about four fifths Baga with Touriga Nacional by its sheet (Wine House Portugal), and the 2019 the same by two merchants; the Rota da Bairrada shop lists one Reserva with Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon and an older listing a third Syrah, so grapes says mostly Baga with Touriga Nacional for recent Reservas.

The six months in French oak after malolactic rest on the 2014 sheet and a 2019 magnum listing; the 2014's further eighteen months in cement and the 2019's pneumatic treading rest on one sheet each and are left out.

The plan's Porta dos Cavaleiros as the house's Dão rests on Blend All About Wine alone, so it is left out of others; the first trade is Douro wines and liqueurs on the house's English page and Port on its centenary page, and the record follows the English page.

The Reserva definition follows the national labelling portaria the Dão refuter read (Portaria 26/2017, consolidated), not read afresh here; the house's claim of the first Reserva is told as its claim.
Living or undated names met, none in the prose: the founders' descendants who led the firm from the late 1950s and the house's winemaker interviewed by a travel blog.

others: Porta dos Cavaleiros, the house's Dão of the end of the 1950s, added on a second account.

wine.name: Quinta das Bágeiras Garrafeira Tinto
wine.grapes: Baga alone, from the family's old vines.
wine.sites: The family's old Baga vines, more than ninety years old; in a year with no Garrafeira all their fruit goes to the Reserva instead.
wine.making: Made only in years the house judges exceptional: the bunches are not destemmed and ferment for five to eight days in open lagares, punched down by hand several times a day. Fermentation ends in old wooden tonéis, where the wine rests for about eighteen months, and it is bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, cranberry and red plum with tobacco leaf and a smoky edge; very firm, grainy tannin from the stems and high, cutting acidity, austere and long.
wine.ageing: Fierce in youth, it wants ten years and more before it opens, and from a strong vintage it lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle two hours ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: A vintage red of marked quality aged at least thirty months, twelve of them in glass, by Portugal's wine law.
The DOC of the coastal plain between the Dão hills and the Atlantic, demarcated in 1979.

records.table: Quinta das Bágeiras Garrafeira Tinto is Baga from vines of more than ninety years near Sangalhos, made only in exceptional years, fermented with its stems in open lagares and aged in old tonéis. Fierce and tart young, it needs years in bottle and a long decant.
records.story: Quinta das Bágeiras lies at Fogueira, in the parish of Sangalhos near Anadia, where the family brought together vineyards handed down from the founder's grandfathers, whose grapes had long been sold in bulk to other wineries. The Bairrada around it was recognised and demarcated in 1979, and a decade later, in 1989, the family began to bottle and sell wine under the estate's own name; the Rota da Bairrada counts the venture the region's first new wine company in more than twenty years. From the start the house kept to the old ways of the region: Baga with its stems, fermented in open lagares, finished and aged in large old wooden tonéis, and bottled without fining or filtering. The Garrafeira, from the old vines, is made only in the years the family judges exceptional; in the others its fruit goes into the Reserva. Its sparkling wines follow the same patience, riddled by hand on wooden pupitres. The word Garrafeira is itself a legal mention: a vintage red of marked quality aged at least thirty months, twelve of them in bottle. For a sommelier the Bágeiras Garrafeira is Baga made the old way and left unsoftened, a wine for the cellar and for the roast meats of the Bairrada.

traps: Garrafeira on a Portuguese red is a legal mention of long ageing, at least thirty months with twelve in bottle, not the name of a vineyard or of a wine shop.
The Bágeiras Garrafeira is not made every year: in the years without one, the old vine Baga goes into the Reserva.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, with two shared with the group (the Bairrada's order of 1979 and the Garrafeira mention); the house's own domain was not found, so its technical sheets hosted by the Rota da Bairrada's shop stand as its primary pages.

The making (not destemmed, five to eight days in open lagares, hand punch downs, finished and aged about eighteen months in old tonéis, unfined and unfiltered, made only in exceptional years with the fruit going to the Reserva otherwise) rests on the house's 2017 Garrafeira sheet and Hedonism; no added yeast rests on the Rota da Bairrada's shop page; the vines of more than ninety years on Hedonism and a second merchant.

Founded is 1989: the Rota da Bairrada calls the project created in 1989 and a merchant's profile says the wines were first bottled and sold that year; the family's three generations before it (one source says four) are told without a year.

The Rota da Bairrada's first new wine company in more than twenty years is told as its account; the sparkling's hand riddling and sugarless liqueur rest on the house's Bruto Natural sheet of 2023, and the Grande Reserva's grapes and lees time are left out (one retailer each).

The glass draws on merchant and press tasting notes of the 2017 and 2018 and on Baga's character; the ageing reflects a published drinking window running to 2040 for the 2017, not quoted because it sits beside a score.
Living names met, none in the prose: the founder of 1989 and the grandfather for whom a wine is named, his dates not found.

wine.name: Casa de Saima Garrafeira Tinto
wine.grapes: Baga, from old vines of about eighty years.
wine.sites: Old Baga vines of about eighty years on the sandy clay soils of the estate's vineyards around Sangalhos.
wine.making: Made only in years the house judges exceptional: fermented in small open lagares, the cap of skins pushed down into the must again and again to draw out colour and tannin; the wine then spends about two years in oak and a further year in bottle before it is released.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, redcurrant and tobacco with damp earth and a smoky edge; firm, dense tannin and vibrant acidity hold it together and promise a long life.
wine.ageing: Built for long ageing, it stays firm through its first decade and, from a strong vintage, opens slowly over many years after.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle well ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Portugal's legal mention for a vintage red of marked quality given at least thirty months of ageing, twelve in glass.
The DOC of the coastal plain around Anadia and Mealhada, named for its clay, barro.
The family estate at Sangalhos; casa means house.

records.table: Casa de Saima Garrafeira Tinto is Baga from vines of about eighty years at Sangalhos, fermented in small open lagares and given two years in oak and a year in bottle before release. Firm and vibrant, it is a Bairrada red for the cellar, so decant it well.
records.story: Casa de Saima is a family estate at Sangalhos, in the heart of the Bairrada near Anadia, which by its own account has made wine for more than half a century, a work handed down across three generations. The region around it, long planted with vines, was recognised and demarcated as Bairrada only by an order of 28 December 1979, and the estate's red wines have been made from Baga, the grape of the region's clay. Saima keeps to the old way with it: the grapes fermented in small open lagares, the cap of skins pushed down into the must again and again, and the reds given long years in wood and in bottle before they are sold. Its Garrafeira, from vines of about eighty years on sandy clay, is the slowest of them, two years in oak and one in bottle, made, as the house says, for long ageing, with firm structure and vibrant acidity. The word on its label is a legal mention: a vintage red of marked quality aged at least thirty months, twelve of them in glass. In 2017 the house tried Pinot Noir, a small experimental bottling that has stayed in its range in small editions. For a sommelier the Saima Garrafeira, from a small family house, shows how the region's traditional Baga is made and how long it asks to wait.

others.name: Casa de Saima Garrafeira Branco
others.note: A white Garrafeira, which Portugal's wine law asks to age at least twelve months, six of them in glass.

others.name: Casa de Saima Pinot Noir
others.note: Begun in 2017 as a small experimental bottling and kept in the range in small editions since.

traps: A white Garrafeira needs at least twelve months of ageing with six in bottle, a red at least thirty with twelve in bottle, so the same word promises different waits.
Saima's Garrafeira is old vine Baga; the house's Reserva is the red that blends Baga with Touriga Nacional, as its label says.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35, two on the house's own domain; this is a thin record by the region rule: a small family estate whose history the house gives only as more than half a century and three generations, so founded is left empty.

The Garrafeira's vines of about eighty years on sandy clay, small open lagares with the skins submerged, 24 months in oak and a year in bottle, rest on the house's own Garrafeira page; Flatiron Wines and the Rota da Bairrada's 2017 Colheita sheet add foot treading and spontaneous fermentation in open lagares, kept out of the making since they are not tied to the Garrafeira.

Left out for want of a second source or for doubt: the Corga vineyard (a review reposted on the house's blog and Flatiron, which adds Barzomba), ageing in hundred year old casks (one listing), the estate left to its present head by her late husband (Flatiron alone), and the Baga Tonel 10, which the house calls a young red and Flatiron a ten year old wine.

The house's own page on the region dates the Bairrada's school of viticulture to 1867 and its first sparkling wine to about 1890; regional history on a producer's page is not the house's own fact, so it is left out pending a second source.
Living names met, none in the prose: the woman who runs the estate and the consultant winemaker named on its sheets, and a writer whose choices the house's blog cites.

records.place: The Buçaco forest near Luso, Mealhada, on the Bairrada's eastern edge

wine.name: Buçaco Reservado Tinto
wine.appellation: Table wine, outside the Bairrada and Dão DOCs
wine.grapes: Baga from the Bairrada and Touriga Nacional from the Dão, in shares that change with the vintage.
wine.sites: Fruit from both sides of the line between the Bairrada and the Dão, Baga from the one and Touriga Nacional from the other; the forest of Buçaco stands on the border.
wine.making: For most of its history the hotel bought finished wines of both regions, then blended and aged them in its own cellar. From about 2000 it bought grapes instead and made the wine itself at Curia nearby, and the red has since spent about a year in 300 litre French oak barrels.
wine.glass: Red cherry and red plum with cedar, tea leaf and dried herbs; fine but firm tannin and bright acidity give more lift than weight and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and fresh when young, it is made for long keeping, and old vintages decades on have long been poured from the hotel's cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant an old bottle gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Buçaco Reservado Tinto is the red of the Bussaco Palace Hotel, whose wines began in 1917 by most accounts: Baga of the Bairrada blended with Touriga Nacional of the Dão. Neither DOC allows that blend, so it is sold as table wine.
records.story: In 1888 work began in the forest of Buçaco on a palace designed by an Italian stage designer and architect, meant, as most accounts tell it, as a royal hunting lodge, though the minister behind the plan had first proposed a hotel. Built in the neo-Manueline style, which recalls the Portuguese age of discovery, it was finished in 1907. The king it was built for was assassinated in Lisbon in 1908 and never stayed there, the monarchy fell in 1910, and by 1917 the palace was a hotel. Its wines began, by most accounts, in 1917, and in 1920 they took the labels, one red and one white, that they have carried with little change ever since. The forest stands where the Bairrada meets the Dão, and the hotel took wine from both sides, Baga from one and Touriga Nacional from the other, a blend neither appellation allows, so its wines have been sold as table wine. For decades they were poured only at the hotel and its owners' other hotels, and from about 2000 the hotel bought grapes rather than finished wine and made the wine itself. For a sommelier, Buçaco is the lesson that a wine of no appellation can carry a long history.

traps: Buçaco's wines are sold as table wine, outside both DOCs, because they blend grapes of the Bairrada and the Dão, not because of any fault in them.
Buçaco and Bussaco are two spellings of one place, the forest and palace near Luso; the hotel is Bussaco, the wines are labelled Buçaco.

questions.exp: By most accounts the hotel's wines began in 1917, with their labels in 1920; in 1897 the palace was under construction and there was no hotel.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share of 35; no page of the hotel's own was found, so every fact rests on two secondary sources and the record has no primary source.

The palace: Wikipedia and a second account give the architect's invitation of 1888, the royal hunting lodge, the neo-Manueline style and completion in 1907; the architect (Luigi Manini) and the minister who invited him are described, not named, since their dates were not found in two sources here.

The hotel's opening is told as soon after 1910: one source credits a concession after the republic, another a 1911 opening by the king's chef, and others say inaugurated in 1917; 1917 for the first wines rests on the importer, Wine House Portugal and others, and the labels of 1920 on the importer and a second merchant.

The grapes vary by account: 60 per cent Baga for one 2015 listing, 60 per cent Touriga Nacional for another 2015 listing, about 80 per cent Baga for Vinha da Mata, so grapes says the shares change; the 300 litre French oak casks rest on the importer and Curry Wines, about a year on Cave Lusa and a second merchant, and the importer's few years in bottle before release is left out.

The label category: Curry Wines prints Vinho de Mesa, the US importer lists the wines as Vinho de Portugal, so the label term gives Vinho de Mesa as the plain table wine category and the checker may prefer the newer wording.

Volatile and left out: the hotel's operation is under a fifty year public concession put to tender in 2024 (Eco, Idealista, Turismo de Portugal), the merger of 2012 and the present partner who sells the wines abroad; if the new concession ends the cellar, the pick may need review, though the wines' history stands.
Living names met, none in the prose: the hotelier family's present members, the cellar's partner, and the writers of the tastings found.
